sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 of the 1905 atlas, drawn at the smaller scale of 120 feet to an inch and oriented with north at the top, unlike the street sheets. It covers the outlying western and northern edge of Como (now Lake Como and the eastern part of Wall Township and Spring Lake Heights), on both sides of the New York and Long Branch Railroad, which crosses the sheet diagonally from the bottom centre to the top right. West of the railroad the country road network dominates: Wall Church Road runs across the upper left with a straggle of small frame dwellings and outbuildings on long lots, Manasquan Turnpike runs down from the north toward Beverly Avenue and St. Clair Avenue at the bottom, and the Road from Bailey's Corner leaves it westward. Along the turnpike stand a hotel, stores and dwellings, the Lake Como M.P. Church near Brand's Road, and the public school at the foot of the sheet. A stream with two ice houses on its bank cuts across the top. East of the railroad stand Como Station and the Como Electric Light Plant, noted as closed for the past seven years, with Pitney Avenue and South Boulevard reaching toward the town. In the lower right the regular grid of Como begins: Worthington, Ludlow and Tuttle Avenues and St. Clair Avenue cross 5th Avenue and 4th Avenue in narrow numbered lots, almost all still vacant. Large tract numbers 101 to 106 label the undeveloped land. The scale bar is printed at the lower left.
notes: Printed scale: 120 ft to an inch; north at the top of the sheet.
Manasquan Turnpike is now Route 71; St. Clair Avenue is Saint Clair Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
Como Electric Light Plant, closed for the past 7 years; Como Station on the railroad.
Lake Como M.P. Church and the public school on the turnpike.
Como outskirts, 120 ft to an inch, north up: Wall Church Road, Manasquan Turnpike, Como Station, Worthington/Ludlow/Tuttle/St. Clair at 5th and 4th Avenues. One part.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 of the 1905 atlas covers the northern, Como end of Spring Lake and the Como district beside it, drawn at 120 feet to an inch with north toward the top of the page. At the left edge the New York and Long Branch Railroad runs diagonally past Como Station, a small pink-coloured station building at the left margin. From the station the wide Pitney Avenue and South Boulevard run east across the sheet, crossed on a diagonal by 3rd Avenue, while Brand's Road and 4th Avenue branch southwest from the junction near the station. Monroe Avenue cuts across the upper right corner with a row of narrow numbered lots. The upper blocks, numbered 101 and 102, are mostly vacant, with a few scattered dwellings, ice houses and outbuildings near Pitney Avenue. The lower half holds a regular grid of narrow platted lots between Vroom, Worthington, Ludlow and Tuttle Avenues, lettered blocks (L, J, F, M, N, G, H) with a scattering of dwellings in 1905 and large undeveloped tracts numbered 103 and 104. The Ann May Memorial Hospital stands at the right edge on the block between Pitney and Vroom Avenues beside 1st Avenue. Overhead wire poles, 4-inch and 6-inch water pipes are marked in the streets, and street widths of 60, 70 and 80 feet are lettered. A compass rose and the 120 foot scale bar occupy the lower left corner; sheet numbers of neighbouring sheets 2, 4 and 6 are printed at the margins.
notes: Printed scale: 120 ft to an inch.
The names on this sheet are unchanged today; Brand's Road may correspond to Brand Parkway but was not used.
Junctions of Monroe Avenue with South Boulevard and of 4th Avenue with Pitney Avenue were left out of the fit (oblique junctions, residuals over 3 m).
Como, 120 ft to an inch, north up: South Boulevard, Pitney, Monroe, Vroom, Worthington, Ludlow, Tuttle Avenues with 1st to 4th Avenues; Como Station at the left edge.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 of the 1905 atlas covers the Como shore, the north end of the settled part of Spring Lake, at 120 feet to an inch with north toward the top. Lake Como lies along the top edge, bounded by South Boulevard, and the Atlantic Ocean forms the right edge, separated from the blocks by Ocean Avenue and the line of the Board Walk. A fan of avenues runs southeast from the lake shore: Pitney, Remsen, Howell, Lorraine, Monroe and Prospect Avenues, with the blocks between them numbered 1 to 15 and subdivided into lots. The few buildings are dwellings, among them the estates marked Seacroft and Seawood; Seawood, with a large brick house under construction, stands on the big block numbered 10 and 11 at the left. Further south the regular grid of 1st Avenue, Vroom, Worthington, Ludlow and Tuttle Avenues carries the lettered blocks B, C and D, including the Globe Block, and Adrian Avenue runs diagonally beside two large blocks numbered 101 and 102. Near the beach at the bottom right a U.S. Life Saving Station and its boat house, with another life saving station further down, stand on or beside Ocean Avenue. Water pipes (4 inch and 6 inch) and street widths are lettered, and the compass rose and 120 foot scale bar are at the lower right.
notes: Printed scale: 120 ft to an inch; the fit gives 3.31 px per foot, consistent with the other 120 ft sheets.
Ocean Avenue was left out of the fit: its junctions carried residuals of 3.4 to 3.8 m, so the beach street is displaced from today's line.
Street names are unchanged in OpenStreetMap (Remsen Avenue, Howell Avenue and the others).

Como by Lake Como, 120 ft to an inch, north up: North/South Boulevard, Remsen, Howell, Lorraine, Monroe, Prospect, Ocean Avenues. Ocean Avenue left out (3.4-3.8 m); fit somewhat distorted (RMSE 2.8 m).

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 of the 1905 atlas covers the Como district west of the railroad, drawn at 120 feet to an inch and turned so that north points to the right of the page (about 77 degrees clockwise). The New York and Long Branch Railroad crosses the sheet from left to right as a broad band of tracks. North of it the Manasquan Turnpike runs across the upper part, with Beverly Avenue and a few blocks of numbered lots (blocks 101 to 103) and scattered dwellings, a lumber shed and building materials yard (Chas. Lewis) beside the tracks near Brighton Avenue, and the Chalfonte Ho. (colored) near the railroad at the left. A large area in the north is blank and marked 100. South of the railroad the grid of Passaic, Morris, Jersey and Washington Avenues, crossed by 5th and 4th Avenues, carries blocks 58, 59, 104, 106, 107 and 108 with a modest number of dwellings, coal pockets beside the track at the left, and a lumber yard and stock yard near Brighton Avenue. St. Clair Avenue and Brighton Avenue run diagonally on the right, with block 105 and 109 divided into narrow numbered lots. A road marked "Road to Bailey's Corner" appears at the upper right. A compass rose and a 120 foot scale bar sit at the lower left.
notes: Printed scale: 120 ft to an inch.
Manasquan Turnpike is today Route 71 and St. Clair Avenue is Saint Clair Avenue; Beverly Avenue and Brighton Avenue keep their names.
The Beverly Avenue and Brighton Avenue junction (oblique) was left out of the fit (4.1 m residual).
Route 71 junctions with Saint Clair and Warren Avenues carry residuals of about 3 m.
West edge, 120 ft to an inch: Manasquan Turnpike, Beverly, Brighton, St. Clair, Warren, Passaic, Morris, Jersey, Washington Avenues, 5th and 4th Avenues; railroad.

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 of the 1905 atlas covers the Como shore blocks south of the railroad district, at 120 feet to an inch, turned so that north points to the right (about 77 degrees clockwise). The Atlantic Ocean occupies the bottom of the page, with the Board Walk drawn as a dashed double line with yellow dashes and Ocean Avenue along the inner edge of the beach. Numbered avenues 4th, 3rd, 2nd and 1st run across the sheet toward the ocean. Washington, Madison and Newark Avenues cross them on the left, while Brighton Avenue, St. Clair Avenue and Tuttle Avenue run diagonally through the right-hand blocks. The blocks (101 to 114, and lettered K, I, E, A) are divided into narrow lots and carry many dwellings, a fairly dense seaside residential district for 1905. The Wilburton, a large hotel with an annex, stands on block 112 near Ocean Avenue, and two small buildings and a larger one stand by the Board Walk, one beside Ocean Avenue at the left and others at the right. Adrian Avenue is lettered at the lower right edge. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inch are marked in the streets with fire hydrant and lamp posts. A compass rose and the 120 foot scale bar are on the right.
notes: Printed scale: 120 ft to an inch.
The Wilburton hotel stands on block 112.
St. Clair Avenue is today Saint Clair Avenue.
The Ocean Avenue and Tuttle Avenue junction was left out of the fit (4.6 m, the beach street is displaced).
Como/Spring Lake beach end, 120 ft to an inch: Washington, Madison, Newark, Brighton, St. Clair, Tuttle Avenues, 1st to 4th Avenues, Ocean Avenue; Wilburton hotel.

sheet-7-1.description: Main part of sheet 7 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas, at 60 feet to an inch, with the ocean side toward the bottom of the page and north toward the upper right. It shows the district west of the railroad, today in Spring Lake Heights, between Manasquan Turnpike along the top edge and the New York and Long Branch Railroad near the bottom. West Ocean Avenue runs along the left edge, Prospect Avenue and Lake Avenue cross the sheet parallel to it, and 1st Avenue crosses them halfway down. The area is lettered as the Rogers Tract and is divided into uniform numbered lots, most still vacant. Buildings are few and mostly frame dwellings and stables; the larger ones front Manasquan Turnpike, among them the Glendale House with its bar at the corner of West Ocean Avenue and a store with the post office further along the turnpike. East of Lake Avenue the North Branch, a stream running to Wreck Pond, winds across the upper right of the part, with two circular ice houses on its bank behind Lake Avenue. A short stretch of the turnpike crosses the stream on a bridge at the top right corner. A heavy line running down from the right edge and then straight down to the bottom separates this part from the Villa Park inset drawn on the same sheet. Below the railroad at the bottom left the edge of the next block south is shown, belonging to sheet 8. A large compass rose and the scale bar are printed on the sheet.
notes: Manasquan Turnpike is now Route 71 (Spring Lake Heights).
West Ocean Avenue is now Ocean Road west of the railroad.
1st Avenue here is now 6th Avenue (Spring Lake Heights).
Glendale House (hotel with bar) at Manasquan Turnpike and West Ocean Avenue; two ice houses on the North Branch.

Two parts: 1 main (Manasquan Turnpike to railroad: Prospect, Lake, 1st [now 6th] Avenues, West Ocean Avenue, Spring Lake Heights); 2 inset at lower right behind a heavy line (Villa Park: Central and Shore Avenues south of West Ocean Avenue, east of the railroad). Part 2 anchored on West Ocean Avenue at the railroad carried from part 1 (its Shore Road junctions were unreliable).

sheet-7-2.description: Second part of sheet 7 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas, drawn at 60 feet to an inch in the lower right of the sheet behind a heavy dividing line, with its own north arrow. It shows the Villa Park section east of the railroad and south of West Ocean Avenue, on the north shore of Wreck Pond, which is not adjacent on the page to the main part of the sheet but continues it across the railroad. The New York and Long Branch Railroad crosses the top of the part. West Ocean Avenue runs down the right edge and Central Avenue down the middle; Shore Avenue enters diagonally from the railroad crossing at the upper left and then curves along the pond shore at the bottom to meet West Ocean Avenue near a bridge. The blocks between Central and West Ocean Avenues hold a handful of large frame dwellings and cottages and the hotel or boarding house called The Brunswick near the railroad. The large triangle between Shore Avenue and the railroad is lettered Villa Park and is largely vacant. Wreck Pond and its feeder stream fill the lower left corner. Water pipes are marked along Shore and West Ocean Avenues with hydrants at the corners. The edge of the block beyond West Ocean Avenue, belonging to sheet 8, shows at the right margin.
notes: Inset placed beside the main part on the sheet; on the ground it lies east of the railroad, across West Ocean Avenue from sheet 8.
West Ocean Avenue is now Ocean Road; Shore Avenue is now Shore Road.
The Brunswick, a large frame building near the railroad.
Placed from one point, West Ocean Avenue at the railroad carried from part 1, with the scale and rotation of part 1.

Two parts: 1 main (Manasquan Turnpike to railroad: Prospect, Lake, 1st [now 6th] Avenues, West Ocean Avenue, Spring Lake Heights); 2 inset at lower right behind a heavy line (Villa Park: Central and Shore Avenues south of West Ocean Avenue, east of the railroad). Part 2 anchored on West Ocean Avenue at the railroad carried from part 1 (its Shore Road junctions were unreliable).

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas, at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean side at the bottom of the page and north toward the upper right. It covers the west end of Spring Lake just east of the railroad, between West Ocean Avenue at the left edge and Atlantic Avenue at the right, from the New York and Long Branch Railroad across the top to 4th Avenue at the bottom. Most of the sheet is taken up by the North Branch, the stream that feeds Spring Lake, which passes under the railroad in two culverts and winds in broad loops across the middle of the sheet before turning down toward the bridge on West Ocean Avenue at the lower left. On the higher ground between the railroad and the stream, part of the Rogers Tract, 2nd Avenue and Prospect Avenue are laid out in a few large lots; the West Windsor and East Windsor boarding houses stand near West Ocean Avenue, with a few dwellings on Prospect Avenue. South of the stream, Salem Avenue and Pennsylvania Avenue run down to 4th Avenue through blocks of narrow numbered lots, nearly all vacant; on 4th Avenue near Pennsylvania Avenue stand the A.M.E. church and a small laundry. The block between Salem and Atlantic Avenues reaches up to 5th Avenue at the right edge. The circular tank of the water works on the neighbouring sheet shows at the upper right. Water pipes are marked in West Ocean Avenue, and the scale bar is printed beside the bridge.
notes: West Ocean Avenue is now Ocean Road; Penna. Avenue is Pennsylvania Avenue.
2nd Avenue and Prospect Avenue east of the railroad have no modern counterpart on their drawn lines (Villa Park Way lies about 34 m off) and were not used.
West Windsor and East Windsor boarding houses; A.M.E. church on 4th Avenue.
Modern Ocean Road east of the railroad is realigned and was left out; West Ocean Avenue at the railroad is carried from sheet 7 part 1.

North Branch between the railroad and 4th Avenue: West Ocean, 2nd, Prospect, Salem, Pennsylvania, Atlantic Avenues. Sparse: 3 detected points plus West Ocean Avenue at the railroad carried from sheet 7-1; modern Ocean Road is realigned (left out). Low confidence (RMSE 3.3 m).

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas, drawn at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean side at the bottom of the page (north toward the upper right). It covers the western part of Spring Lake between 5th Avenue and 4th Avenue, from Atlantic Avenue at the left edge to Sussex Avenue at the right, with Monmouth Avenue and Essex Avenue crossing the sheet. The New York and Long Branch Railroad runs across the top of the sheet in a broad multi-track right of way, with a freight house on its south side near Sussex Avenue. North of 5th Avenue, beside the railroad, stands the Spring Lake Water Works: an elevated 80,000 gallon tank, an engine house with gasoline engines and pumps, a buried 300 gallon gasoline tank, and a note that water comes from two driven wells with direct pressure for fire. A small town storage building stands nearby, and the North Branch, a tidal stream feeding Spring Lake, loops through the upper left block. South of 5th Avenue the blocks between Atlantic, Monmouth, Essex and Sussex Avenues are laid out in uniform narrow lots, numbered but almost entirely vacant in 1905. The one large building is St. Ann's Roman Catholic church on the west side of the block between Atlantic and Monmouth Avenues, with a small dwelling on the opposite side of the street. Water pipes are marked along 5th Avenue and the cross avenues, with hydrants at intervals. Block numbers 52 to 54 and 63 to 65 are printed in the blocks, and the scale bar sits in 4th Avenue at the bottom edge.
notes: Printed scale: 60 ft to an inch.
Spring Lake Water Works with an 80,000 gallon elevated tank, supplied from two driven wells.
St. Ann's R.C. Church between Atlantic and Monmouth Avenues.
The railroad is lettered New York and Long Branch R.R.; today the North Jersey Coast Line.
Pilot. 5th to 4th Avenue, Atlantic to Sussex Avenues; water works; railroad. 60 ft to an inch.

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 of the 1905 atlas shows the middle of Spring Lake town at 60 feet to an inch, turned so that north points toward the upper right (about 77 degrees clockwise). The New York and Long Branch Railroad crosses the top as a band of tracks with the Depot, a pink-coloured station building with a baggage building and news stand, on its south side. Between the railroad and 5th Avenue, blocks 60 and 62 hold the commercial centre of 1905: a plumber, W. D. Robinson's wind mill and plumbing shop, a carpenter shop, the Colonnade, a boarding house, a lock-up, C. W. Simonson's bottling works, and a fire house with a steam fire engine, hook and ladder truck and hose wagon. The centre block 61 is a park-like square with a circle and diagonal paths. South of 5th Avenue the blocks 55 and 56 contain a few dwellings, the Public School, St. Andrew's M.E. Church and the Spring Lake Golf & Country Club building, while Spring Lake itself, a narrow tidal pond, curves through the lower right, bounded by Warren Avenue and Passaic Avenue. Mercer, Warren, Sussex and Passaic Avenues run across the sheet and 4th Avenue at the bottom. Street widths and water pipes are lettered, and the compass rose is at the upper left.
notes: Printed scale: 60 ft to an inch.
The railroad, lettered New York and Long Branch R.R., is today the North Jersey Coast Line.
The sheet shows a public school, St. Andrew's M.E. Church and the Spring Lake Golf & Country Club.
5th to 4th Avenue, Sussex to Passaic Avenues; railroad, golf club, school, church.

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean side at the bottom of the page. It shows the south-western edge of Spring Lake between 4th Avenue at the top and 2nd Avenue at the bottom, from West Ocean Avenue and Wreck Pond at the left to Atlantic Avenue at the right. Pennsylvania Avenue and Salem Avenue cross the sheet between them, and 3rd Avenue divides it across the middle. The blocks, numbered 27 to 29 and 47 to 49, are laid out in narrow numbered lots and are almost entirely vacant. The only buildings are in the block between 3rd and 2nd Avenues east of Salem Avenue: Timothy Hurley's livery, sale and exchange stable, with a carriage house, wagon shed and several smaller frame buildings, and two small dwellings further east along Atlantic Avenue. Wreck Pond, a tidal creek, runs down the left side of the sheet, widening towards the bottom, and its irregular bank cuts across the lots beside West Ocean Avenue. A compass rose stands in the lower left corner with the scale bar below it. Water pipes are marked at the street ends with their widths, and the street widths are lettered as 60 and 80 feet. The adjoining sheets are numbered 8 above, 12 at the right and 15 below, and their numbers are printed in the margins.
notes: Printed scale: 60 ft to an inch.
West Ocean Avenue corresponds to today's Ocean Road, but the modern road is far closer to Pennsylvania Avenue than the drawn one, so it was not used as control.
Timothy Hurley's livery stable stood on the block between 3rd and 2nd Avenues, east of Salem Avenue.
4th to 2nd Avenue, West Ocean to Atlantic Avenues by Wreck Pond. West Ocean Avenue (Ocean Road) left out: modern road displaced.

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean side at the bottom of the page. It covers the area between 4th Avenue at the top and 2nd Avenue at the bottom, from Atlantic Avenue at the left to Sussex Avenue at the right, with Monmouth Avenue and Essex Avenue crossing it and 3rd Avenue across the middle. The lots in the blocks numbered 30, 31, 32, 44, 45 and 46 are partly built up. Most buildings are frame dwellings with porches, scattered along Monmouth Avenue and in the block west of it, together with a number of stables and outbuildings. An Episcopal church stands in the upper left block on the west side of Monmouth Avenue, and St. Catherine's Roman Catholic church, drawn in pink as a masonry building, stands in the block east of Essex Avenue facing 3rd Avenue. At the lower right West Lake Avenue curves away from Essex Avenue along the shore of Spring Lake, whose blue outline crosses the lower right corner, and a second branch of the water with East Lake Avenue appears at the very bottom edge. Water pipes with their sizes and hydrants are lettered along the avenues. A compass rose stands at the top left and the scale bar at the bottom. Sheets 9, 11, 13 and 16 adjoin; their numbers are printed in the margins.
notes: Printed scale: 60 ft to an inch.
West Lake Avenue curves with the lake shore; it was not used as control.
The church at the upper left is lettered Episcl Church; the pink church at the right is St. Catherine's R.C. Church.
4th to 2nd Avenue, Atlantic to Sussex Avenues; Episcopal and St. Catherine's R.C. churches.

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas, at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean side at the bottom of the page and north toward the upper right. It covers the middle of Spring Lake itself, the long narrow lake that gives the town its name, between 4th Avenue across the top and 2nd Avenue across the bottom, from Sussex Avenue at the left edge to Passaic Avenue at the right. The lake enters from the lower left, widens across the centre of the sheet and turns up toward the top right in a narrow arm, and a long foot bridge carries the line of Mercer Avenue across it. West Lake Avenue follows the north shore and East Lake Avenue the south shore, with Mercer Avenue and Warren Avenue running down to them from 4th Avenue and from 2nd Avenue. The blocks are laid out in uniform numbered lots and hold scattered large frame cottages of two and a half stories, set well apart, with a few stables and outbuildings; the blocks along 4th Avenue near Sussex Avenue and between Mercer and Warren Avenues near 2nd Avenue are the most built up. Much of the land by the lake is open. Water pipes with hydrants are marked in 4th Avenue, Warren Avenue, Passaic Avenue and 2nd Avenue. Block numbers 34, 35, 42 and 43 are printed, and the edge of sheet 17 appears below 2nd Avenue. The scale bar is printed at the bottom left.
notes: A foot bridge crosses the lake on the line of Mercer Avenue.
Junctions on the curved lakeside avenues (Mercer / West Lake, Warren / East Lake) disagreed by 4 to 5 m and were left out.
Spring Lake (the lake) between 4th and 2nd Avenues, Sussex to Passaic Avenues; foot bridge.

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 of the 1905 atlas shows the business centre of Spring Lake at 60 feet to an inch, turned so that north points toward the upper right (about 77 degrees clockwise). It covers four numbered avenues running across the page, 4th, 3rd and 2nd Avenues, crossed by Passaic, Morris, Jersey and Washington Avenues, with the blocks numbered 36 to 40 and 101 in a grid of narrow platted lots. The densest building lies along 3rd Avenue: livery stables (Jos. T. Smith, McCue and Beecroft, and Henry Osborn), a furniture, crockery and glassware store, a steam laundry, a tin shop, a drug store and a bakery, and an auto repairing and storage garage. The Spring Lake Water Works stands in block 101 near Washington Avenue with an elevated tank, a double cylinder engine, hose cart and hose; a printed note along the right margin describes the force pump, the reservoir and direct pressure for fire. A bank with a hot water system, an ice cream factory and several smithies and carpenter shops are drawn, while the outer blocks hold dwellings and vacant lots. Water mains of 4, 6 and 8 inch are lettered along the avenues. The sheet carries a compass rose at the top and a 60 foot scale bar at lower left.
notes: Printed scale: 60 ft to an inch.
Spring Lake Water Works with an elevated tank and a fire house.
Street names are unchanged in OpenStreetMap.
4th to 2nd Avenue, Passaic to Washington Avenues.

sheet-15.description: Sheet 15 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean at the bottom of the page. It shows the beach side of Spring Lake from 2nd Avenue at the top through 1st Avenue to Ocean Avenue, and from Union Avenue at the left to Atlantic Avenue at the right, with Pennsylvania Avenue and Salem Avenue between. Wreck Pond occupies the upper left corner, where its channel turns across the corner of the sheet. The blocks, numbered 3 to 5 and 22 to 24, are divided into narrow lots and are largely vacant. The one large building is The Allaire, a hotel of three and a half storeys with elevated verandas on posts, standing at the left on the block south of 1st Avenue. A grocery or similar small building and a few dwellings stand elsewhere. Along the beach at the lower right a walled enclosure holds the bath houses, drawn as a grid of small cabins with a larger building among them, and a pavilion stands just south of the Boardwalk, which runs the width of the sheet as a yellow and white striped band. The Atlantic Ocean forms the bottom edge. A compass rose is at the upper left, with the scale bar at the bottom. The adjoining sheets 11, 16 and 23 are numbered in the margins.
notes: Printed scale: 60 ft to an inch.
Union Avenue is not used as control: modern Union Avenue lies only about 27 m from Pennsylvania Avenue, while the drawn avenues are about 115 m apart.
Ocean Avenue junctions were left out of the fit because the beach side of the street is not drawn, and the points made the fit worse (1.2 m against 0.2 m RMSE).
The Allaire is the hotel at the left; the Boardwalk and a bath house enclosure lie along the beach.
2nd Avenue to the beach, Union to Atlantic Avenues; Allaire hotel, bath houses. Control only in the top two rows (Ocean and Union Avenues left out).

sheet-16.description: Sheet 16 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean at the bottom of the page. It covers the central beach district from 2nd Avenue at the top to Ocean Avenue and the Boardwalk, between Atlantic Avenue at the left and Sussex Avenue at the right, with Monmouth Avenue and Essex Avenue crossing it and 1st Avenue across the middle. Spring Lake itself fills the upper centre, a curving blue water with West Lake Avenue on its western shore and East Lake Avenue on its eastern shore, and a compass rose stands in the lake outline. The hotels are the main buildings. The Hotel Ruskin and the Palmer House stand in the upper left block, The New Monmouth, a large cross-shaped hotel drawn in pink as a brick or stone building with a service wing, stands beside Ocean Avenue, and the Essex and Sussex Hotel and Cottages occupy the lower right block between Essex and Sussex Avenues with its annexes. A Presbyterian church stands east of the lake. A note beside The New Monmouth lists its steam heating, electric lights, water tanks and fire pumps and says it is open only during the season. The Boardwalk runs across the bottom above the Atlantic Ocean edge. The scale bar is at the lower right.
notes: Printed scale: 60 ft to an inch.
2nd Avenue meets Essex Avenue and Sussex Avenue in no modern junction, since the lake and the lake avenues intervene.
West Lake Avenue and East Lake Avenue follow the lake shore and were not used as control.
Hotels: Hotel Ruskin, Palmer Ho., The New Monmouth, and the Essex & Sussex Hotel & Cottages.
2nd Avenue to the beach, Atlantic to Sussex Avenues; Monmouth House and other hotels by the lake.

sheet-17.description: Sheet 17 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean at the bottom of the page. It covers the blocks from 2nd Avenue at the top, across 1st Avenue, to Ocean Avenue and the Boardwalk, between Sussex Avenue at the left and Passaic Avenue at the right, with Mercer Avenue and Warren Avenue between. The corner of Spring Lake and East Lake Avenue show in the upper left corner. The blocks numbered 7 to 9 and 16 to 18 are among the more built-up in the atlas, with many frame cottages and boarding houses with porches, stables and small outbuildings. The Colonial Hotel stands in the left block north of 1st Avenue, and The Breakers, a large frame hotel with annexes, stands in the block south of 1st Avenue between Sussex and Mercer Avenues. The blocks next to Ocean Avenue are laid out in narrow lots and many are still vacant. Beyond Ocean Avenue lies open beach, with a small building near the Boardwalk, the Boardwalk drawn as a pair of dashed lines, and the Atlantic Ocean along the bottom edge. A compass rose stands at the lower right and the scale bar at the lower left. Water pipes and hydrants are marked along the avenues.
notes: Printed scale: 60 ft to an inch.
East Lake Avenue appears only in the upper left corner and was not used as control.
Hotels: Colonial Hotel and The Breakers.
2nd Avenue to the beach, Sussex to Passaic Avenues; Colonial Hotel, The Breakers.

sheet-18.description: Sheet 18 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean at the bottom of the page. It covers the north-eastern end of the beach district from 2nd Avenue at the top, across 1st Avenue, to Ocean Avenue and the Boardwalk, between Passaic Avenue at the left and Washington Avenue at the right, with Morris Avenue and Jersey Avenue between. The blocks, numbered 10 to 15, are divided into narrow lots and are built up mainly with frame dwellings and cottages in the blocks north of 1st Avenue, while the blocks south of it hold fewer buildings. The Spring Lake Casino, a large building with a tower and an annex, stands in the middle block south of 1st Avenue, between Morris and Jersey Avenues. The Berk Cottage stands at the upper right. Ocean Avenue runs across the lower part of the sheet with open beach beyond, the Boardwalk drawn as dashed lines with yellow marks, and a small structure beside it. The Atlantic Ocean forms the bottom edge. A compass rose is at the top and the scale bar at the lower right. Water pipes, hydrants and the widths of the streets are lettered along the avenues.
notes: Printed scale: 60 ft to an inch.
The Casino is lettered Spring Lake Casino; the cottage at the upper right is lettered The Berk Cottage.
2nd Avenue to the beach, Passaic to Washington Avenues; Spring Lake Casino.

sheet-23.description: Sheet 23 of the 1905 Spring Lake atlas, at 60 feet to an inch with the ocean at the bottom of the page and north toward the upper right. It covers the southern end of Spring Lake between Wreck Pond at the top and the Atlantic Ocean at the bottom, from South Avenue on the left to Union Avenue on the right, with York Avenue between them. 1st Avenue crosses the sheet below the pond, and at its left end a bridge leads across Wreck Pond to Sea Girt. Ocean Avenue runs along the beach at the bottom; only its inland edge is drawn, with open beach between it and the shoreline. The four blocks are laid out in uniform lots and numbered 1, 2, 25 and 26, but they were almost empty in 1905: the only buildings are a fish house on the block between South and York Avenues facing Ocean Avenue and, on the beach at the lower right, a small frame building and an open-sided shed. The shore of Wreck Pond curves across the top of the sheet and down its left edge to the bridge. Water pipes are marked in 1st Avenue with hydrants at the corners. A compass rose and a scale of feet are printed on the sheet; this sheet was added to the Spring Lake series and continues the numbering after the Sea Girt sheets.
notes: South Avenue appears to be today's Brown Avenue, but the modern street lies about 6 m off the drawn line and was left out of the fit.
Bridge to Sea Girt at the west end of 1st Avenue across Wreck Pond.
Ocean Avenue is drawn with only its inland edge; the Ocean Avenue points rest on an assumed street width.
South end by Wreck Pond: South (now Brown, displaced), York, Union Avenues, 1st and Ocean Avenues; bridge to Sea Girt. Sparse; added after the Sea Girt sheets 19-22 (separate record).
